Run the agent in a container that Suspense owns, so each mode sees only what
it may use. The isolation comes from what is mounted, not from prompts, deny
rules or guards. Spec tasks, a chain's spec step and questions always run
this way. Code tasks and a chain's code step run this way only when the
project's "Run code tasks in a container" option is on (off by default); when
it is off they run on the host as today, with the mode guard and read-deny
rule.

Why: Spec work keeps reading and even changing code, which wastes time and
tokens, and the chain's code step then finds nothing to do. Deny rules and
prompt wording are only nudges, because a shell can read anything. A
container that has no code in it can't read the code or change it, whatever
the harness is and whatever it tries.

What should be true afterwards:

1. Container runtime: Podman only, run through the `podman` CLI. Each run is
   one `podman run --rm` of the agent's command, a child of the app, so
   stopping a task stops its container. On Linux it runs rootless with the
   user's id (--userns=keep-id), so files it writes belong to the user. On
   macOS and Windows, Podman runs in a `podman machine`.
   - If `podman` isn't installed, a Spec, Chain or Ask prompt isn't sent, and
     there is no unisolated fallback. The task or question says Podman is
     needed and links to Podman's installation instructions for the platform
     it's running on: https://podman.io/docs/installation#macos on macOS,
     https://podman.io/docs/installation#windows on Windows, and
     https://podman.io/docs/installation#installing-on-linux on Linux. It's
     reported the way a missing harness or missing piton is today.
   - On macOS and Windows, if no Podman machine exists or it isn't running,
     the task says so and offers to set it up (`podman machine init`) or
     start it (`podman machine start`), showing the output in its raw stream.
   - Code tasks with the project option on need Podman in the same way. With
     the option off, they never need it.

2. Image. Suspense builds a default image and keeps it up to date: the
   harness CLIs (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode) and piton, the same versions
   as on the host where it can find them. A project can provide its own
   Containerfile (.suspense/Containerfile) built FROM the default to add
   toolchains, and Suspense builds and caches it when it changes, with
   `podman build`. While an image is building, the task shows "Preparing
   environment" and the output goes to its raw stream.

3. What each run sees. Mounts are made at the same absolute paths as on the
   host where the platform allows, so paths in tool events need no mapping.
   Where they can't be (macOS, Windows), container paths are mapped back to
   host paths everywhere they are shown or opened (referenced-spec sidebar,
   file links, understanding file, files changed).
   - Spec task, chain spec step: the spec location rw, the compiled
     reference rw, the fluency file ro, piton.config.pi ro, and the task's
     understanding file rw. No code location.
   - Question (Ask): the code location ro, the compiled reference ro, and
     piton.config.pi ro. No spec source. Nothing writable but the harness's
     own volumes.
   - Code task, chain code step, with the option on: the code location rw,
     the compiled reference ro, piton.config.pi ro, and the understanding
     file rw. No spec source.
   Nothing else from the host is mounted: no home directory, no user-level
   skills, MCP servers or ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, no git directory. Snapshots,
   diffs, files changed and commits are still done by Suspense on the host.

4. Persistent Podman volumes, owned and named by Suspense:
   - one per harness for its login and settings (~/.claude, ~/.codex,
     OpenCode's data directory), shared by every project, so a harness is
     logged in once for all of them;
   - one per project and conversation lane (spec lane, code lane,
     questions) for the harness's sessions, so each lane can resume its own
     conversation;
   - caches per project (e.g. cargo registry and target directory) for
     containerised Code runs.
   Losing a volume costs only a login or a cache, never project data.

5. Logging in. When a harness in its volume isn't logged in, Suspense runs
   its login command in the container under a pseudo-terminal and shows a
   login view. It opens any login URL the CLI prints in the host's browser.
   Where the CLI asks for a pasted code, the view has a field for it, which
   goes to the PTY. Where it waits for a localhost callback on a known port,
   that port is published for the login run. Where it offers device-code
   login, that is used. Credentials stay in the harness's volume and are
   refreshed there, so login happens once per machine, not per run. The
   Settings window shows each harness's container login state and has a
   "Log in again" action.

6. Conversations by lane. Spec lane tasks (Spec tasks and chain spec steps)
   carry on a conversation of their own, separate from the code lane's, so
   nothing a code task read reaches a spec task. Questions keep their own
   conversation as today. The chain handoff stays as text (the prompt and
   the spec step's reply), so it crosses lanes unchanged. New conversation
   resets the lane it is used from.

7. The spec build. A Spec run's agent can run `piton build` inside its
   container (the code location isn't there, so shape outputs written into
   it are discarded). After every Spec or chain spec step, Suspense runs the
   real `piton build` on the host as it does before sending, so the host's
   reference and shape outputs are current.

8. Prompts describe only what the run can see. For containerised runs, the
   system template, the spec-reading prompt and the mode instructions no
   longer name a location the run can't see, or tell it not to read or edit
   one: Spec and chain-spec-step instructions don't name the code location,
   and Ask and containerised Code instructions say the spec is read from
   the compiled reference without naming the spec source. The shared system
   prompt stays identical within a lane's conversation, so the prompt cache
   holds.

9. Guards. A containerised run has no mode guard, no read-deny rule and no
   edit-deny rule: nothing to protect is mounted. Host runs (Code with the
   option off, Freeform) keep them as today.

10. Project option. "Run code tasks in a container" is a per-project
    setting, saved with the project as the ProjectDataScope says, shown in
    the Settings window, off by default. Turning it on applies from the next
    Code or chain code step.

Spec: harness-integration (how a run is started, conversations and
resuming, Claude Code's flags), prompt-mode/index and prompt-mode/sending
(lanes, chains, the pre-send build, the mode guard), prompt-mode/
mode-system-prompts (what each mode's prompts say), project-data (the new
option, Containerfile, and which data is the project's vs. Suspense's),
settings-window (the option and the harness login state), and spec-build
(the build after a spec step). Update those anchors rather than adding
parallel ones. Add one new scope for the container environment (Podman,
the missing-Podman and machine states with their platform install links,
image, mounts per mode, volumes, login), and link to it from the others.

Code: put the container environment in its own module (Podman detection and
machine state, platform install links, image build and cache, mounts per
mode, volume names, path mapping, the login PTY flow), used by
src/harness.rs where the agent's Command is built, for send, one-off runs
and ask_quickly alike when their mode is containerised. Update
src/mode_guard.rs so containerised runs aren't guarded, src/system_prompts.rs
and .suspense/system-prompts/*.md for the prompt wording, the conversation
bookkeeping in src/prompt_mode.rs and src/conversations.rs for the separate
spec-lane conversation, src/settings_window.rs for the option and login
state, and src/referenced_spec.rs and src/shell_paths.rs for path mapping.
Tests: mounts per mode (Spec has no code mount, Ask has no spec mount and
nothing rw, Code only with the option on), the missing-Podman error linking
to the right install page per platform, the machine-not-running state on
macOS and Windows, the spec lane resuming its own conversation, no guard or
deny rule for containerised runs, and container-to-host path mapping. Use a
fake `podman` binary, as the existing tests use a fake harness.

# Harness Integration Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

Uses the one-off version of a coding harness for the selected ProjectDirectoryScope: `claude -p`, `codex exec`, or `opencode run`, whichever the user chose. Each run carries on a conversation, so the harness keeps its context between requests.

### Shape

#### Description

Should always run in auto mode.
The project's system prompt, its system template filled in, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope) says, is appended to the harness's own system prompt, for example with `--append-system-prompt`, the same for every prompt of a conversation whatever its mode. The compiled systemPrompt of a prompt's hidden anchor, its mode's instructions, heads the prompt's own message instead.
The prompt is given to the harness on its standard input, and what the harness does is streamed back as it happens. A task's run takes its prompt as a stream of messages rather than a single one, so it can be fed more while it works, as its feeding says.
Its directory, which a system prompt's HARNESS_DIRECTORY stands for, is that of the harness in use: .claude, .codex, or .opencode.

#### Harnesses

The harness in use is the one picked in the [SettingsWindowScope](../settings-window/index.md#settings-window-scope): Claude Code, Codex, or OpenCode, Claude Code until another is picked. It is remembered for the user, as the [UserPreferencesScope](../user-preferences/index.md#user-preferences-scope) says, not for a project. Every run the application starts goes to it, the tasks, the questions, the palette's file search, the one-off runs, and the notes, commit messages, and prompt titles it writes, and everything else works the same whichever it is. A run already going when another is picked finishes with the harness it started with, and a conversation is only carried on by the harness it began with; the next request with another harness starts a new one.
Each harness is run its own way, streaming what it does as a line of JSON per event, which is read into the same reply, tool calls, usage, and result, whichever harness wrote it:

- Claude Code is `claude -p`, in auto mode, the system prompt given with `--append-system-prompt`, a conversation carried on with `--resume`, and a copy of one with `--fork-session`.
- Codex is `codex exec`, with `--full-auto` and `--json`, the prompt read from its standard input, a conversation carried on with `resume`.
- OpenCode is `opencode run`, with `--format json`, a conversation carried on with `--session`.

Codex and OpenCode take no system prompt of their own, so it is given ahead of the prompt, marked off from it. Neither can carry on a copy of a conversation, so a question asked while another is running starts a new conversation with them instead. The notes, commit messages, and prompt titles are written with a small model where the harness can be told one, Claude Code's haiku, and with the harness's default model otherwise.
When the harness picked isn't installed, a run fails saying that it can't be run, as any run that can't be started does.

#### Protected Locations

Where the harness takes rules for what its tools may do, as Claude Code does with `--disallowedTools`, a run is told what its mode keeps it off. A Code task is told it may not edit the spec location, and a Spec task the code location; the application puts back whatever changes there all the same, and says so in the task's output as a passive notice, never an error, as the [TaskTableScope](../../ui/components/task-table/index.md#task-table-scope) says. A Code task and a question from the Ask tab are also told they may not read the spec location, alongside that, so they read the compiled reference instead, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope) says. This rule is only a nudge, and doesn't enforce anything, since a shell command can still read the files, and nothing puts anything back or stops the run when one does. A harness that takes no such rules is told nothing of either.

#### Feeding

A task's run is given its prompt as a stream of messages: Claude Code with `--input-format stream-json`, each message written as a line of JSON on the harness's standard input, which stays open for as long as the run lasts. The run's first message is the task's compiled prompt, as ever, and each message sent to the task after it, from the [ChatInputScope](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope), is written as another.
A message reaches the harness when it finishes what it is doing rather than interrupting it, so a run that is mid-tool-call takes it once that call is over. The harness echoes each message back as it takes it in, with `--replay-user-messages`. A message taken in between turns is answered with a result of its own, and one taken while a turn is under way is answered within that turn, sharing its result.
A run can also start work in the background that goes on after its turn ends: Claude Code's subagents, shell commands run in the background, such as a long build, and any other kind of background task it adds later. Every such task holds the run open, whatever its kind. The run keeps each background task that has started and not yet ended, by its id: one starts when the harness says a task has started, and ends when the harness notifies that task's end, whatever it ended as. A notification doesn't say what kind of task it is, so it is matched by id against those seen starting. The harness wakes the run when a background task ends, so it can act on what came of it.
A result no longer ends the task on its own. The run's last result is the first to come once every message sent has been taken in and no background task is still going. A result that comes before then, while a message sent hasn't been taken in or a background task is still going, is only an answer: the task keeps running, its input stays open, and more can still be sent to it. At the last result the run's input is closed, but the task is only shown as finished once the harness's process has exited as well, and it then finishes in the state of that last result; until the process exits, the task keeps running. A process that exits without a last result finishes the task as a run with no result does, failed. A run that is stopped closes its input and ends straight away, whatever is still going in the background, since its whole process group is ended with it.
Codex's `codex exec` and OpenCode's `opencode run` read a single prompt and can't be fed more while they work, so a task running with either takes its prompt as ever and can't be sent more.
Questions, the palette's file search, the one-off runs, and the notes, commit messages, and prompt titles each take a single prompt, as ever.

#### Images

Images attached to a prompt, as the [ChatInputScope](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope) says, are given to the harness as it takes them: to Claude Code as image content blocks, base64-encoded with their media type, in the same stream-json user message as the prompt's text, after it; to Codex with an `--image` argument per image; and to OpenCode with a `--file` argument per image. A message fed to a running Claude Code task carries its images the same way, and a Claude Code run that isn't fed more but has images is given its prompt as a stream-json message too, so the images can go with it. ## Concept

### Shape

#### Description

#### On Its Own

#### Projects

A build run on its own belongs to the project it started in, as the [OpenProjectsScope](../open-projects/index.md#open-projects-scope) says, and carries on when switching to another project. The command shows it running only while that project is on screen; another project can build at the same time. When it is over while another project is on screen, its notification's title ends with the name of the project it built, such as "Built 3 files in my-project".

A build ahead of other work runs when that work actually starts, not when it is asked for, and shows as a step of that work until it is over. It isn't listed among the running activity on its own, since the work it leads is.

## Concept

### Pitch

### Shape

#### Description

It replies with nothing but JSON, shaped as its prompt asks, which each use describes.

#### Failing

When the harness can't be run, fails, or replies with something that can't be read as that JSON, the run fails, with why. Each use says what it does then.

#### Stopping

Closing whatever started it stops it.

# Prompt Sending Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

How a prompt gets to the harness, whether written in the chat input or sent on the application's behalf.

### Shape

#### Description

A prompt is sent in one of the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope), with anything attached to it. Sending is never blocked by the harness working.

#### Tasks

A task, a prompt in Code, Chain, Spec, or Freeform, is sent straight away while its lane is free. While its lane is busy, it waits in its queue instead, in the order it was sent, keeping its mode and attachments, until its turn comes.
When a task is actually sent, the spec is built ahead of it, as the [SpecBuildScope](../../spec-build/index.md#spec-build-scope) says, the task showing "Building" until the build is over; then its hidden anchor is compiled and run. It heads the [MessageList](../message-list/index.md#message-list) as the latest task, and is saved in the prompt history, as the [ProjectDataScope](../../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says. A prompt that fails to compile or run fails its task, and doesn't stop its queue.

#### Lanes

Tasks run in two lanes, the code lane and the spec lane, each with a queue of its own, so work on the spec never waits on work on the code, or the other way round. A task sent in Code goes to the code lane, and one sent in Spec to the spec lane. A Chain task's steps each go to the lane of the work they do, as the [PromptEditor](../index.md#prompt-editor) says: its spec steps to the spec lane and its code step to the code lane, even though they were sent together from the Chain tab. A task sent in Freeform may change either, so it goes to the code lane, and is only sent while no task runs in either lane; while it runs, both lanes are busy, and prompts for either queue behind it.
A lane is busy while a task of its own is building, compiling, or running, or a Freeform task is. So a Spec task sent while only a Code task runs is sent straight away and runs beside it, and a Code task sent while only a Spec task runs does the same; a task only queues behind a task of its own lane. At most one task runs in each lane, and each lane's queue sends its prompts one at a time, first to last. Both lanes belong to the same project, and a project's lanes only ever send into that project.

#### Questions

A question, a prompt in Ask, never queues: it runs straight away, even while the harness is working on a task or other questions, joins the questions stacked above the [ChatInputScope](../chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope)'s tabs, and is saved among the questions asked.

#### Sending To ATask

While a task is running, more can be sent to it, as to a terminal session, from the [ChatInputScope](../chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope)'s "Send to task", as it says. It goes to the latest task, whose output is shown; a task running in the other lane, among the previous tasks, isn't sent to. What is sent is written as a hidden anchor and compiled like any prompt, unless the task was sent from Freeform, when it goes just as it was typed, with its attachments, its references, attachments, and Slice toggle included, so it can reference the spec, but the spec isn't built first, and its systemPrompt isn't sent, since the run already has the one it began with. It goes to the running task's run as a message of its own, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, and is not a task of its own: it doesn't head the [MessageList](../message-list/index.md#message-list), isn't among the previous tasks, and can't be resent. It is shown in the task's output and kept with its record, as the [PromptEditor](../index.md#prompt-editor) says. A message that fails to compile isn't sent, and a notification titled "Could not send to the task" says why, what was typed going back into the input. A message whose task ends before it can be sent is queued instead, as a task, so nothing typed is lost.

#### On The Applications Behalf

Something in the application can send a prompt as if it were written in the chat input and sent from one of its tabs. It goes just the same

##### Way

queued if its lane is busy, shown as a task, and entered in the

history. What is being written in the chat input, and attached to it, is left alone.

#### Resending

A prompt sent before can be sent again, from a Resend button: a small ghost button with a rotating-arrow icon, whose tooltip says it sends the prompt again as it was sent. It sits at the right of the latest task's header, and of the heading of each previous task and previous answer, beside its chevron; clicking it never opens or closes the item.
Resending sends the prompt as it was typed, in the mode it was sent in, with the text that was attached to it, and sliced or not as it was, as though it were sent afresh from the chat input: a task queues while its lane is busy, a question runs straight away, and either is compiled anew, against the spec and system prompt as they are now, building the spec first as any task does, and saved in the history as a new task or question. The prompt resent stays where it is. A prompt whose mode isn't known, saved before modes were, is resent from the chat input's selected tab. What is being written in the chat input, and attached to it, is left alone, and so is the Slice toggle.

#### Cancelling

A task under way can be cancelled, from a Cancel button: a small ghost button with a stop icon, whose tooltip says "Cancel this task", at the right of the latest task's header, beside its Resend button, shown only while the task is building, compiling, or running. With a task running in each lane, the one that isn't the latest task shows among the previous tasks as Running, with the same Cancel button at the right of its heading, beside its Resend button, and clicking it never opens or closes the item. A task is cancelled straight away, whatever the harness is in the middle of: a build or compile under way is abandoned before the task is run, and a run is stopped, the harness's process ended, not left to finish its turn.
A cancelled task keeps the output it had so far, and its status reads "Cancelled", as the [MessageList](../message-list/index.md#message-list) shows, in the history as much as in its header. It adds no commit note, and any change the harness had already made to files is left as it is. Its lane's queue carries on after it, as it does after a task that fails, sending the next prompt waiting in it, and the next task carries on the same conversation. The task in the other lane, and questions, are not cancelled with it.

#### Sending To The Other Mode

A task sent in Code alone can be sent to Spec, and one sent in Spec alone can be sent to Code, from a small ghost button beside its Resend button, tinted the colour of the mode it sends to, whose tooltip says "Send to Spec" or "Send to Code". It sits wherever Resend does for a task, at the right of the latest task's header and of the heading of each previous task, and clicking it never opens or closes the item. Tasks sent in Chain, questions, and prompts whose mode isn't known don't offer it.
Sending to the other mode is resending, as above, in every way but the

##### Mode

the prompt is sent in the other mode, with that mode's system

prompt, and saved in the history as a new task in that mode.
A Code task sent to Spec is also told what the code task did, so the spec can be written from it. Its system prompt is Spec's, followed, on a paragraph of its own, by the code-to-spec prompt of the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope), which says that the prompt was first sent to change the code, and now the spec is to be written to describe what was built, and holds the code task's prompt, as it was typed, and its final

##### Output

the reply text after the code task's last tool call, all of it

when it made none. A code task that left no final output, having failed, been cancelled, or said nothing after its last tool call, is said to have left none. Its user prompt is the prompt as typed, as for any resend.
The new Spec task remembers the code task it was sent from, in its history record, so resending it sends it the same way, with the same prompt and final output, and its header shows, beneath the hidden anchor's name, that it was sent from Code. A Spec task sent to Code is sent with Code's system prompt alone.
A task that has been sent to the other mode no longer offers to be sent there once that has succeeded, and every task sent in Code or Spec alone keeps its button in the same place either way: once the task sent from it has finished as Done, its Send to Spec or Send to Code button is greyed out and disabled, in the latest task's header and in its heading among the previous tasks, its tooltip reading "Sent to Spec" or "Sent to Code". The batch actions neither count nor send it, though it can still be selected. While the task sent from it is waiting in the queue, building, compiling, or running, the button is disabled too, its tooltip reading "Being sent to Spec" or "Being sent to Code", so it isn't sent twice. If that task fails, is cancelled, or is left "Not recorded", as when the application closed while it ran, or a queued prompt sent from it is cancelled, the button is enabled again. A resend of the task sent from it counts the same: once any task sent from it finishes as Done, the button is disabled. ##### Way

queued if its lane is busy, shown as a task, and entered in the

history. What is being written in the chat input, and attached to it, is left alone.

# Project Data Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

What the application keeps for a project, kept in the project itself so it survives a restart and travels with the project.

### Shape

#### Description

Everything the application keeps for a project lives in a `.suspense` directory inside the [ProjectDirectoryScope](../project-directory/index.md#project-directory-scope), created as it is needed. Nothing about a project is kept anywhere else, apart from the draft.

#### Contents

- `history/`: every task sent, as its hidden anchor's source, named by the second it was sent and the anchor's name, and beside it, once its run is over, a `.json` record of the same name holding the compiled userPrompt the harness received, the system prompt as it received it and the harness it went to, whether it has been marked done by hand for sending to the other mode, each line the harness printed, each message sent to the task while it ran, in its place among those lines, any error, and, in a git repository, the hashes of the two snapshots of the working tree taken as it started and ended, as the task snapshots below say
- `snapshot-index`: in a git repository, the private index the task snapshots are built with, as they say
- `images/`: every image attached to a task or question, saved when it is sent or queued, named by the second it was saved and a short hash of its content, with its own extension, so the same image attached twice is saved once
- `asks/`: every question asked from the Ask tab, saved the same way as a task but apart from them
- `queue/`: each queued prompt, as its hidden anchor's source, imports included, named so they list in the order they were queued, marked when each was queued rather than when it was saved, so prompts queued one straight after another keep their order however long each takes to save
- `divergence/`: each divergence report, a JSON file named by when it was made
- `system-prompts/`: each mode's system prompt template, a Markdown file named after its mode, code.md, combined.md for Chain, spec.md, and ask.md, and the spec-reading prompt injected into them, spec-reading.md
- `commit-notes.json`: the Git panel's commit notes
- `run.json`: the project's run targets, as the [RunTargetsScope](../run-targets/index.md#run-targets-scope) says
- `harness.json`: the last report the harness gave of the skills and agents it has
- `fluency.md`: the project's Piton fluency, as `piton agent --print-fluency` printed it at the last spec build, generated rather than edited, for the Spec and Chain prompts to point at, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope) says
- `conversations.json`: which conversation of the tasks, and of the questions, was last left for a new one, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, so it isn't carried on again once the project is reopened

The draft, `.suspense-draft.pi`, isn't in `.suspense`: it is the prompt being written, as `piton lsp` is shown it, a document named as if it were in the spec location, as the [ProjectLocationsScope](../project-locations/index.md#project-locations-scope) says, so the server resolves its imports.

#### Machine Only

Some of it belongs to one machine rather than to the project: the harness report `.suspense/harness.json`, the fluency `.suspense/fluency.md`, printed by this machine's piton, the queue `.suspense/queue/`, the commit notes `.suspense/commit-notes.json`, the conversations left `.suspense/conversations.json`, whose conversations only this machine's harness knows, the snapshot index `.suspense/snapshot-index`, and the draft `.suspense-draft.pi` wherever it is, should it ever be written. Git ignores these, so they are never committed. Everything else, the prompt history, the questions, the divergence reports, and the system prompts, is kept with the project.

#### Task Snapshots

In a project that is a git repository, every task the harness runs keeps a record of the files that changed while it ran. When the harness actually starts the task, not when it is sent or queued, the project's working tree is snapshotted, and it is snapshotted again when the run is over, however it ends: done, failed, or cancelled. In a project that isn't a git repository, nothing is snapshotted or recorded, and nothing about it is shown anywhere.
A snapshot is a git tree, made with git's plumbing alone: `git add -A` and then `git write-tree`, run with `GIT_INDEX_FILE` pointing at a private index, `.suspense/snapshot-index`, so the repository's own index, HEAD, branches, stash, and working tree are never read from or written to. A snapshot follows `.gitignore`, as git does, so ignored files, `.suspense`'s machine-only data among them, are never in it. No commit, branch, worktree, or stash is ever made, nothing is added to the user's history, and no tool but git is needed.
Both trees are pinned so git's garbage collection never deletes them, each under a private ref, `refs/suspense/<task>/before` and `refs/suspense/<task>/after`, `<task>` being the task's hidden anchor's name, and their hashes are kept in the task's history record. A snapshot that can't be taken, as when git fails, is left out rather than stopping the task; a task missing either snapshot shows no changed files.
The private index and the refs belong to this machine: `snapshot-index` is ignored by git like the other machine-only data, and the refs are never pushed, since nothing pushes `refs/suspense/`.

#### Reading

What can't be read is left out, or shown as missing, rather than stopping the rest from being read.

#### Last Project

When the application starts, it opens the project that was opened most recently, the first of the [ProjectDirectoryScope](../project-directory/index.md#project-directory-scope)'s recent projects that still holds its piton.config.pi. With none, it starts with no project open.

A SettingsWindowScope should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase. The editor grows to fit the prompt, as a [GrowingTextInputScope](../../ui/components/growing-text-input/index.md#growing-text-input-scope) does, with no most, so it never scrolls on its

##### Own

the whole prompt is always in it, and the page scrolls instead,

the mouse wheel over an editor scrolling the page. A prompt that can't be read or saved says why beneath its editor.
Without a project open, as the [NoProjectStateScope](../no-project/index.md#no-project-state-scope) says, in place of the prompts it reads "Open a project to edit its system prompts."

#### Injected Prompts

The "Injected prompts" section is headed "Injected prompts", with a muted line beneath saying that these are injected into the system prompts wherever their placeholder is written, that they are saved with the project as they are edited, and that HARNESS_DIRECTORY stands for the directory of the harness in use, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope) says.
Then the spec-reading prompt, laid out as each tab's system prompt is: its name, "Spec reading", the muted path of the file it is saved in, a "Reset to default" button, disabled while it is already the default, its editor, and why it can't be read or saved, if it can't. Beneath it the code-to-spec prompt, laid out the same way, named "Code to spec", with a muted line saying it is added to a Code task sent to Spec, and that CODE_PROMPT and CODE_RESULT stand for the code task's prompt and its final output.
Without a project open, in place of it the section reads "Open a project to edit its injected prompts."

#### Agent

The "Agent" section is headed "Agent", with a muted line beneath saying that every run, the tasks, the questions, and the application's own, goes to the harness picked here, and that a conversation is only carried on by the harness it began with.
Then a row for each harness, in order: Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode, each a radio button reading its name, with the command it runs muted beside it, `claude`, `codex`, or `opencode`, and "Not installed" muted after that when the command can't be found. Exactly one is picked, the harness in use, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says. Clicking one picks it; it is used from the next run on, and remembered for the user straight away, as the [UserPreferencesScope](../user-preferences/index.md#user-preferences-scope) says, not saved with a project, so the section is the same with or without a project open. One that isn't installed can still be picked, and its runs fail saying why.

#### Saving

The prompts, the system prompts and the injected ones, belong to the project opened through the [ProjectDirectoryScope](../project-directory/index.md#project-directory-scope), each saved with the project's data, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says. The prompts are read again each time the settings open and whenever another project is opened, so an edit made by hand shows up; a prompt that already shows what was read is left alone, so its cursor stays put.

#### Templates

A prompt is a template, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope) says, and a reset puts back its default.

use /lib
from /scope/harness-integration import HarnessIntegrationScope
from /scope/project-data import ProjectDataScope

export scope ContainerEnvironmentScope:
    concept: {ContainerEnvironmentConcept}

concept ContainerEnvironmentConcept:
    pitch:
        A container the application owns, that a run of the harness works
        in, so each mode sees only what it may use. What a run can read or
        change comes from what is mounted into its container, never from its
        prompt, a deny rule, or a guard: a container with no code in it can't
        read the code or change it, whatever the harness is and whatever it
        tries.

    shape: {ContainerEnvironmentShape}

shape ContainerEnvironmentShape:
    description:
        Spec tasks, a Chain prompt's spec steps, and questions from the Ask
        tab always run in a container. Code tasks and a Chain prompt's code
        step run in one only while the project's "Run code tasks in a
        container" option is on, as the @{ProjectDataScope} says; while it is
        off, they run on the host as ever, as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope}
        says, with its protected locations. Freeform tasks always run on the
        host, and so do the application's own runs, the one-off runs, the
        palette's file search, and the notes, commit messages, and prompt
        titles, which change nothing.

        Whatever runs in a container, the application itself still works on
        the host: it builds the spec before a task, takes the task's
        snapshots and lists the files it changed, shows diffs, and makes
        commits there, as ever.

    runtime:
        The container runtime is Podman, run through the `podman` command,
        and no other. Each run is one `podman run --rm` of the harness's
        command, run as a child of the application, given its prompt on its
        standard input and streaming back what it does on its output, just as
        a run on the host does, so stopping or cancelling a run stops its
        container with it, and nothing is left behind once it is over.

        On Linux, Podman runs rootless, and the container runs as the user,
        with `--userns=keep-id`, so every file a run writes belongs to the
        user, as it would on the host. On macOS and Windows, Podman runs its
        containers in a Podman machine, a virtual machine it manages.

    missingPodman:
        Where `podman` isn't installed, a prompt that has to run in a
        container isn't sent, and never runs on the host instead: a Spec task,
        a Chain prompt's steps, a question, and, while the project's option is
        on, a Code task. It fails as a run whose harness isn't installed
        does, as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says, or as one whose spec
        build can't run piton does, its output saying that Podman is needed to
        run it, with a link to Podman's installation instructions for the
        platform the application is running on, opened in the browser when
        clicked:

        - on macOS, https://podman.io/docs/installation#macos
        - on Windows, https://podman.io/docs/installation#windows
        - on Linux, https://podman.io/docs/installation#installing-on-linux

        While the project's option is off, a Code task never needs Podman,
        and runs whether it is installed or not.

    podmanMachine:
        On macOS and Windows, a run also needs a Podman machine that is
        running. Where there is none, the task or question says so, and
        offers to set one up, a button reading "Set up Podman" that runs
        `podman machine init` and then `podman machine start`. Where there is
        one that isn't running, it says that, and offers to start it, a
        button reading "Start Podman" that runs `podman machine start`.
        Either shows what the command prints in the task's raw output as it
        runs, and once it succeeds, the prompt is sent again, as resending
        it would; one that fails says why, as a failed run does. On Linux
        there is no machine, and nothing about one is shown.

    image:
        Runs use an image the application builds itself, with `podman build`,
        and keeps up to date: the default image, holding the harness
        commands, Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode, and piton, each at the
        version installed on the host where it can be found there, and at its
        latest otherwise. It is built again when any of those versions
        changes.

        A project can add to it with a Containerfile of its own,
        `.suspense/Containerfile`, built FROM the default image, to add the
        toolchains its code needs, as the @{ProjectDataScope} says. The
        project's image is built from it, and kept, and built again only when
        the Containerfile or the default image changes. Without one, the
        project's runs use the default image.

        While an image is being built for a run, the task or question shows
        "Preparing environment" as its status, and what the build prints goes
        to its raw output. A build that fails fails the run, saying why.

    mounts:
        What each run sees is what is mounted into its container, and nothing
        else from the host. Each is mounted at the same absolute path it has
        on the host, where the platform allows it, so the paths the harness
        reports in what it does need no mapping, and the run works in the
        project directory's path, as a run on the host does. What each kind of
        run is given, as the @{ProjectLocationsScope} names the locations:

        spec:
            A Spec task, or a Chain prompt's spec step or spec follow-up: the
            spec location, read and write; the compiled reference, the
            harness directory's reference folder, read and write, so it can
            run `piton build` itself; the fluency file, read only;
            piton.config.pi, read only; and the task's understanding file,
            read and write. Never the code location.

        question:
            A question from the Ask tab: the code location, the compiled
            reference, and piton.config.pi, each read only. Never the spec
            location. Nothing is writable but the harness's own volumes.

        code:
            A Code task, or a Chain prompt's code step, while the project's
            option is on: the code location, read and write; the compiled
            reference and piton.config.pi, read only; the task's
            understanding file, read and write; and the project's caches.
            Never the spec location.

        Nothing else is ever mounted: not the user's home directory, the
        user's own skills, MCP servers, or user-level CLAUDE.md, and not the
        project's git directory. A location that holds another, as a code
        location holding the spec or the project data, is mounted without
        the one it holds, so the one held is never seen through it.

    paths:
        Where a mount can't be at the host's path, as on macOS and Windows,
        where the container sees the project at a path of its own, every path
        a run reports from its container is mapped back to its host path
        before it is shown or opened anywhere: the referenced spec in the
        right sidebar, file links in the task's output, its understanding
        file, the files it changed, and what its tool calls touched. A path
        that maps to nothing on the host is shown as the run gave it, and
        opens nothing.

    volumes:
        What a harness keeps between runs is kept in Podman volumes the
        application owns and names, never in the project:

        - one per harness, for its login and settings, ~/.claude, ~/.codex,
          or OpenCode's data directory as the harness keeps it, shared by
          every project, so each harness is logged in once for all of them
        - one per project and conversation, the spec lane's, the code lane's,
          and the questions', for the harness's sessions, so each carries on
          its own conversation, as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says
        - the project's caches, such as the cargo registry and target
          directory, for its Code tasks run in a container

        Losing a volume costs only a login or a cache, never anything of the
        project's.

    loggingIn:
        When the harness isn't logged in, in its volume, the application runs
        its login command in a container, under a pseudo-terminal, and shows
        a login view in an inset panel, titled for the harness, with what the
        command prints. Any login URL the command prints opens in the host's
        browser. Where the command asks for a code to be pasted, the view has
        a field for it, and what is entered there goes to the command. Where
        the command waits for a callback on a known localhost port, that port
        is published for the login run. Where it offers to log in with a
        device code, that is how it logs in. The run waiting on the login is
        sent once the login succeeds, and fails, saying so, if it is
        cancelled or fails.

        The credentials stay in the harness's volume, and are refreshed
        there, so a harness is logged in once on a machine, not for every
        run. The @{SettingsWindowScope} shows whether each harness is logged
        in in its container, and can log it in again.

    guards:
        A run in a container has no protected locations, as the
        @{HarnessIntegrationScope} names them: it isn't guarded, and its
        harness is given no rule against reading or editing any location,
        since nothing it mustn't touch is there. Its prompts, as the
        @{ModeSystemPromptsScope} says, name only what it can see. Runs on
        the host keep their protected locations as ever.

    specBuild:
        A Spec run can run `piton build` in its container, to check its work
        in the refreshed reference; with no code location there, what that
        build writes into the code location, the shape's guidance, goes
        nowhere. Once a Spec task or a Chain prompt's spec step is over,
        however it ended, the application runs `piton build` on the host, as
        the @{SpecBuildScope} says, so the host's reference and shape guidance
        are those of the spec as the run left it.

        ahead of the prompt, marked off from it. Neither can carry on a copy of
        a conversation, so a question asked while another is running starts a
        new conversation with them instead. The notes, commit messages, and
        prompt titles are written with a small model where the harness can be
        told one, Claude Code's haiku, and with the harness's default model otherwise.

        When the harness picked isn't installed, a run fails saying that it
        can't be run, as any run that can't be started does.

    protectedLocations:
        Where the harness takes rules for what its tools may do, as Claude
        Code does with `--disallowedTools`, a run is told what its mode keeps
        it off. A Code task is told it may not edit the spec location, and a
        Spec task the code location; the application puts back whatever
        changes there all the same, and says so in the task's output as a
        passive notice, never an error, as the @{TaskTableScope} says. A Code task and a question from the Ask
        tab are also told they may not read the spec location, alongside that,
        so they read the compiled reference instead, as the
        @{ModeSystemPromptsScope} says. This rule is only a nudge, and
        doesn't enforce anything, since a shell command can still read the
        files, and nothing puts anything back or stops the run when one does. A harness that
        takes no such rules is told nothing of either.

    feeding:
        A task's run is given its prompt as a stream of messages: Claude Code
        with `--input-format stream-json`, each message written as a line of
        JSON on the harness's standard input, which stays open for as long as
        the run lasts. The run's first message is the task's compiled prompt,
        as ever, and each message sent to the task after it, from the
        @{ChatInputScope}, is written as another.

        A message reaches the harness when it finishes what it is doing rather
        than interrupting it, so a run that is mid-tool-call takes it once that
        call is over. The harness echoes each message back as it takes it in,
        with `--replay-user-messages`. A message taken in between turns is
        answered with a result of its own, and one taken while a turn is under
        way is answered within that turn, sharing its result.

        A run can also start work in the background that goes on after its
        turn ends: Claude Code's subagents, shell commands run in the
        background, such as a long build, and any other kind of background
        task it adds later. Every such task holds the run open, whatever its
        kind. The run keeps each background task that has started and not yet
        ended, by its id: one starts when the harness says a task has started,
        and ends when the harness notifies that task's end, whatever it ended
        as. A notification doesn't say what kind of task it is, so it is
        matched by id against those seen starting. The harness wakes the run
        when a background task ends, so it can act on what came of it.

        A result no longer ends the task on its own. The run's last result is
        the first to come once every message sent has been taken in and no
        background task is still going. A result that comes before then, while
        a message sent hasn't been taken in or a background task is still
        going, is only an answer: the task keeps running, its input stays
        open, and more can still be sent to it. At the last result the run's
        input is closed, but the task is only shown as finished once the
        harness's process has exited as well, and it then finishes in the
        state of that last result; until the process exits, the task keeps
        running. A process that exits without a last result finishes the task
        as a run with no result does, failed. A run that is stopped closes its
        input and ends straight away, whatever is still going in the
        background, since its whole process group is ended with it.

        and can't be fed more while they work, so a task running with either
        takes its prompt as ever and can't be sent more.

        Questions, the palette's file search, the one-off runs, and the notes,
        commit messages, and prompt titles each take a single prompt, as ever.

    images:

        to the harness as it takes them: to Claude Code as image content blocks,
        base64-encoded with their media type, in the same stream-json user
        message as the prompt's text, after it; to Codex with an `--image`
        argument per image; and to OpenCode with a `--file` argument per image.
        A message fed to a running Claude Code task carries its images the same
        way, and a Claude Code run that isn't fed more but has images is given
        its prompt as a stream-json message too, so the images can go with it.
        Codex's options end with `--` before the prompt when it is given
        images. Questions take images as tasks do.

    context:
        The harness keeps its context between requests instead of starting fresh
        each time. Tasks share one ongoing conversation, and each task sent
        carries it on. A task that starts while a task of the other lane is
        running, as the @{PromptSendingScope} lets it, carries on a copy of
        that conversation as it was when it started, as a question does, so
        tasks running at the same time never write over each other; the
        conversation tasks carry on afterwards is that of whichever task
        finished most recently. When the project is opened, tasks carry on the latest
        conversation in its history. Questions from the Ask tab share a separate
        conversation of their own, and when the project is opened they carry on
        the latest conversation among the questions saved with it. A question
        asked while another is running carries on a copy of that conversation,
        so questions running at the same time never write over each other. A
        conversation is only carried on in the project it began in, each open
        project keeping its own tasks' and questions' conversations while it is
        in the background, and if one
        can't be carried on, the next request starts a new one. Each run applies
        its own prompt's systemPrompt, even when it carries on a conversation
        begun in a different mode. The palette's file search always starts
        fresh.

        conversation button, as the @{ChatInputScope} says: the next request
        starts a new conversation with no context, and the one left is not
        carried on again, not by a run of it still going, nor by the project's
        history. Leaving it is kept with the project, as the @{ProjectDataScope}
        says, so a project opened after its tasks' or questions' conversation
        was left starts a new one too, rather than carrying on the latest
        conversation in its history, until a run after the reset begins one of
        its own. How much context a conversation holds is
        known from what the harness reports with each reply: everything the
        model was given, cached or not, and what it wrote, as of its latest
        reply; replies of subagents don't count.

concept ModeSystemPromptsConcept:
    pitch:
        The system prompt each mode sends, which tells the harness what kind of
        work a prompt is, and which each project can make its own.

    shape: {ModeSystemPromptsShape}

shape ModeSystemPromptsShape:
    description:
        What a prompt tells the harness besides itself comes in two parts. The
        system template is the conversation's system prompt: the same for
        every prompt of a conversation, whatever its mode, so the harness's
        prompt cache holds when the mode changes. Each of the
        @{PromptModesScope} but Freeform has instructions of its own, which
        change from one prompt to the next, and so go in the prompt's own
        message, in a block marked <task-instructions> at its head. A
        prompt's hidden anchor has a systemPrompt property, alongside its
        userPrompt, holding its mode's instructions.

    templates:
        The system template, each mode's instructions, and the injected
        prompts are Piton prose, like the prompt they are sent with, so they
        can reference the spec, with these placeholders, each written after a
        dollar sign and inside braces like a Piton interpolation:

        - CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION, the code location and the spec location, as the @{ProjectLocationsScope} says
        - HARNESS_DIRECTORY, the directory of the harness in use
        - SPEC_READING, the spec-reading prompt, injected where it is written
        - PITON_FLUENCY_FILE, the path of the fluency file, from the project directory, as the pitonFluency below says
        - UNDERSTANDING_FILE, the path of the task's understanding file

        SPEC_READING is filled in first, so the placeholders it holds are
        filled in too; then the others, before the prompt is compiled, but
        UNDERSTANDING_FILE, which is filled in as the prompt is sent, once the
        task's history record is named, so a prompt sent from the queue is
        given its own. A question from the Ask tab has no understanding file,
        and UNDERSTANDING_FILE is filled in with nothing. Each can be moved or
        removed, like any other text of a template.

        A paragraph that held nothing but a placeholder filled in with
        nothing goes with it. A paragraph holding PITON_FLUENCY_FILE, filled
        in with nothing, goes too, whatever else it says, so a sentence
        pointing at a fluency file there is none of is never sent. A template
        left with nothing but blank space once filled in gives nothing at
        all.

        HARNESS_DIRECTORY is the directory the harness that runs the prompt,
        as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says, reads its agentic Markdown and
        reference files from, written without a leading ./: .claude for
        Claude Code, .opencode for OpenCode, and .codex for Codex, the
        directories the @{NewProjectScope} names for them.

        In every mode, the harness learns what the spec says from its
        compiled reference, the Markdown the spec build writes under
        HARNESS_DIRECTORY's reference folder, where inheritance, expressions,
        and links are already resolved, or, for one thing, from what
        `piton slice` prints for it with the adapter of the harness in use.

        the spec says. The system template and the spec-reading prompt say
        so, and name the spec location only as where edits to the spec go.

    writingTheSpec:
        Only Spec, and a Chain prompt's first step, which writes the spec,
        work on the Piton source. Their instructions say to open a .pi file
        only to change it, since a harness may need a file read before it can

defaults:
        The defaults are the prompts saved in this application's own
        repository, in its `.suspense/system-prompts` directory, named as a
        project's are. They are the source of truth for the defaults, and are
        baked into the application when it is built, so a build always ships
        with whatever those files say, and changing them changes the defaults
        the next build has. A build can't be made without them.

        The system template's default says what the project is, where its
        code and spec are, that each prompt starts with a <task-instructions>
        block saying what that prompt is for and what it may change, and then
        SPEC_READING on a paragraph of its own. It holds no fluency.

        The spec-reading prompt's default says:

        \\
        Read the spec from its compiled reference under ${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference, where inheritance, expressions, and links are already resolved, or, for one thing, from what `piton slice` prints for it with this harness's adapter. Never read the .pi source under ${SPEC_LOCATION} to learn what the spec says; that is only where edits to the spec go.

        Before executing anything, read the spec it touches. Links to ${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference/... in the prompt are the spec for what they name. Read each one you need before changing anything it covers. Don't re-read something you've already read.
        \\

        The Spec and Chain defaults have, after what the mode is for, on a
        paragraph of its own:

        \\
        Before creating or editing any .pi file, read ${PITON_FLUENCY_FILE} once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Piton is written.
        \\

        and then, on another:

        \\
        Open a .pi file only to change it. Once you have changed the spec, run `piton build` and check the result in the refreshed reference under ${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference, not by reading the source again.
        \\

        The Code, Chain, and Spec defaults then end with, on a paragraph of
        its own:

        \\
        Before changing anything, write the constraints this task must meet to ${UNDERSTANDING_FILE}, and keep it current as you read more of the spec. It is a Markdown list and nothing else: one line per constraint, at most twelve, each a single short, specific statement of what must be true, written as a link to the compiled reference file it comes from, such as `- [The chain tab has no bottom border in combined mode](${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference/scope/prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chain)`. Only list what the spec says; leave out anything you are deciding yourself. Replace a constraint when you learn it was wrong rather than adding another.
        \\

        The Ask default says only what a question may and may not change.

        The defaults are only where a project starts, and what resetting a
        prompt puts back. A project whose prompts were saved before a default
        changed keeps them as they are.

# Container Environment Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

A container the application owns, that a run of the harness works in, so each mode sees only what it may use. What a run can read or change comes from what is mounted into its container, never from its prompt, a deny rule, or a guard: a container with no code in it can't read the code or change it, whatever the harness is and whatever it tries.

### Shape

#### Description

Spec tasks, a Chain prompt's spec steps, and questions from the Ask tab always run in a container. Code tasks and a Chain prompt's code step run in one only while the project's "Run code tasks in a container" option is on, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says; while it is off, they run on the host as ever, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, with its protected locations. Freeform tasks always run on the host, and so do the application's own runs, the one-off runs, the palette's file search, and the notes, commit messages, and prompt titles, which change nothing.
Whatever runs in a container, the application itself still works on the host: it builds the spec before a task, takes the task's snapshots and lists the files it changed, shows diffs, and makes commits there, as ever.

#### Runtime

The container runtime is Podman, run through the `podman` command, and no other. Each run is one `podman run --rm` of the harness's command, run as a child of the application, given its prompt on its standard input and streaming back what it does on its output, just as a run on the host does, so stopping or cancelling a run stops its container with it, and nothing is left behind once it is over.
On Linux, Podman runs rootless, and the container runs as the user, with `--userns=keep-id`, so every file a run writes belongs to the user, as it would on the host. On macOS and Windows, Podman runs its containers in a Podman machine, a virtual machine it manages.

#### Missing Podman

Where `podman` isn't installed, a prompt that has to run in a container isn't sent, and never runs on the host instead: a Spec task, a Chain prompt's steps, a question, and, while the project's option is on, a Code task. It fails as a run whose harness isn't installed does, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, or as one whose spec build can't run piton does, its output saying that Podman is needed to run it, with a link, opened in the browser when clicked, to Podman's installation instructions for the platform it is running on:

- on macOS, https://podman.io/docs/installation#macos
- on Windows, https://podman.io/docs/installation#windows
- on Linux, https://podman.io/docs/installation#installing-on-linux

While the project's option is off, a Code task never needs Podman, and runs whether it is installed or not.

#### Podman Machine

On macOS and Windows, a run also needs a Podman machine that is running. Where there is none, the task or question says so, and offers to set one up, a button reading "Set up Podman" that runs `podman machine init` and then `podman machine start`. Where there is one that isn't running, it says that, and offers to start it, a button reading "Start Podman" that runs `podman machine start`. Either shows what the command prints in the task's raw output as it runs, and once it succeeds, the prompt is sent again, as resending it would; one that fails says why, as a failed run does. On Linux there is no machine, and nothing about one is shown.

#### Image

Runs use an image the application builds itself, with `podman build`, and keeps up to date: the default image, holding the harness commands, Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode, and piton, each at the version installed on the host where it can be found there, and at its latest otherwise. It is built again when any of those versions changes.
A project can add to it with a Containerfile of its own, `.suspense/Containerfile`, built FROM the default image, to add the toolchains its code needs, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says. The project's image is built from it, and kept, and built again only when the Containerfile or the default image changes. Without one, the project's runs use the default image.
While an image is being built for a run, the task or question shows "Preparing environment" as its status, and what the build prints goes to its raw output. A build that fails fails the run, saying why.

#### Mounts

What each run sees is what is mounted into its container, and nothing else from the host. Each is mounted at the same absolute path it has on the host, where the platform allows it, so the paths the harness reports in what it does need no mapping, and the run works in the project directory's path, as a run on the host does. What each kind of run is given, as the [ProjectLocationsScope](../project-locations/index.md#project-locations-scope) names the locations:

##### Spec

A Spec task, or a Chain prompt's spec step or spec follow-up: the spec location, read and write; the compiled reference, the harness directory's reference folder, read and write, so it can run `piton build` itself; the fluency file, read only; piton.config.pi, read only; and the task's understanding file, read and write. Never the code location.

##### Question

A question from the Ask tab: the code location, the compiled reference, and piton.config.pi, each read only. Never the spec location. Nothing is writable but the harness's own volumes.

##### Code

A Code task, or a Chain prompt's code step, while the project's option is on: the code location, read and write; the compiled reference and piton.config.pi, read only; the task's understanding file, read and write; and the project's caches. Never the spec location.

Nothing else is ever mounted: not the user's home directory, the user's own skills, MCP servers, or user-level CLAUDE.md, and not the project's git directory. A location that holds another, as a code location holding the spec or the project data, is mounted without the one it holds, so the one held is never seen through it.

#### Paths

Where a mount can't be at the host's path, as on macOS and Windows, where the container sees the project at a path of its own, every path a run reports from its container is mapped back to its host path before it is shown or opened anywhere: the referenced spec in the right sidebar, file links in the task's output, its understanding file, the files it changed, and what its tool calls touched. A path that maps to nothing on the host is shown as the run gave it, and opens nothing.

#### Volumes

What a harness keeps between runs is kept in Podman volumes the application owns and names, never in the project:

- one per harness, for its login and settings, ~/.claude, ~/.codex, or OpenCode's data directory as the harness keeps it, shared by every project, so each harness is logged in once for all of them
- one per project and conversation, the spec lane's, the code lane's, and the questions', for the harness's sessions, so each carries on its own conversation, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says
- the project's caches, such as the cargo registry and target directory, for its Code tasks run in a container

Losing a volume costs only a login or a cache, never anything of the project's.

#### Logging In

When the harness isn't logged in, in its volume, the application runs its login command in a container, under a pseudo-terminal, and shows a login view in an inset panel, titled for the harness, with what the command prints. Any login URL the command prints opens in the host's browser. Where the command asks for a code to be pasted, the view has a field for it, and what is entered there goes to the command. Where the command waits for a callback on a known localhost port, that port is published for the login run. Where it offers to log in with a device code, that is how it logs in. The run waiting on the login is sent once the login succeeds, and fails, saying so, if it is cancelled or fails.
The credentials stay in the harness's volume, and are refreshed there, so a harness is logged in once on a machine, not for every run. The [SettingsWindowScope](../settings-window/index.md#settings-window-scope) shows whether each harness is logged in in its container, and can log it in again.

#### Guards

A run in a container has no protected locations, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) names them: it isn't guarded, and its harness is given no rule against reading or editing any location, since nothing it mustn't touch is there. Its prompts, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope) says, name only what it can see. Runs on the host keep their protected locations as ever.

#### Spec Build

A Spec run can run `piton build` in its container, to check its work in the refreshed reference; with no code location there, what that build writes into the code location, the shape's guidance, goes nowhere. Once a Spec task or a Chain prompt's spec step is over, however it ended, the application runs `piton build` on the host, as the [SpecBuildScope](../spec-build/index.md#spec-build-scope) says, so the host's reference and shape guidance are those of the spec as the run left it.

content.text:
The spec now describes running the harness in a Podman container that Suspense owns, so each mode can only see what's mounted for it. I didn't touch the code. `piton check` reports no problems, `piton build` wrote 76 files, and `piton reach` confirms the new scope is reached.

**New scope: `spec/scope/container-environment/index.pi` (`ContainerEnvironmentScope`)**
- **Which runs are containerised:** Spec tasks, a chain's spec steps and questions always are. Code tasks and a chain's code step are only when the project option is on. Freeform and the app's own runs (one-off runs, file search, notes, commit messages, titles) stay on the host. Snapshots, files changed, diffs and commits are still done on the host.
- **Runtime:** Podman only, one `podman run --rm` per run as a child of the app, rootless with `--userns=keep-id` on Linux, in a Podman machine on macOS and Windows.
- **Missing Podman:** the prompt isn't sent and never falls back to the host. Its output links the install page for the current platform, the three URLs you gave.
- **Podman machine (macOS and Windows):** a "Set up Podman" button runs `podman machine init` then `start`; a "Start Podman" button runs `podman machine start`. Output goes to the raw stream, and the prompt is resent once it works.
- **Image:** a default image built with `podman build`, with harness and piton versions matching the host where they can be found. A project can add `.suspense/Containerfile` FROM it, and that image is rebuilt only when it changes. While building, the task shows "Preparing environment".
- **Mounts per mode:** as in your brief, at host paths where the platform allows. Nothing else is mounted: no home directory, user skills, MCP servers, user-level CLAUDE.md or git directory.
- **Path mapping, volumes, login view, guards, and the build:** as you described.

**Changes to existing scopes**
- **Harness integration:** containerised runs are linked from Description and Harnesses. Protected Locations now applies only to host runs. Context now has one conversation per lane plus the questions'. Turning the option on or off starts the code lane on a new conversation, because its sessions live in different places.
- **Sending:** the Tasks paragraph covers containerised tasks and the host build after spec work. The Questions paragraph says every question runs in a container.
- **Prompt editor:** Chained Tasks says where each step runs and that the handoff stays as text. Building The Spec covers the build after a spec step.
- **Chat input:** the context figure and New conversation work per lane, with four tooltip wordings. The `newConversation` property refers to the task's own lane.
- **Spec build:** a new After Spec Work section.
- **Mode system prompts:** a run fills `CODE_LOCATION` or `SPEC_LOCATION` in with nothing when it can't see that location, and any paragraph holding it goes. The system template's default and the spec-reading default now put each location on a paragraph of its own.
- **Project data:** adds `settings.json` (`runCodeTasksInContainer`, false when absent) and `Containerfile`, both kept with the project. `conversations.json` now tracks each lane. Images and volumes belong to the machine and are never in `.suspense`.
- **Settings window:** a new "Containers" section shows Podman's status, each harness's container login state with "Log in again", and the project checkbox.

**Decisions I made that your brief didn't settle**
- **Understanding file:** it's mounted on its own, so the app creates it empty just before the run. An empty file shows as "not written yet".
- **Freeform with the option on:** it runs on the host but carries on the code lane's conversation, so its system prompt is filled as a containerised Code run's is, without the spec location.
- **Chain tab:** New conversation from the Chain tab resets both lanes, and its context figure shows the spec lane's conversation.
- **Build after a spec step:** the task shows "Building" until it finishes, and a failed build only adds a passive notice to the output.
- **Default prompt files:** the repo's own `.suspense/system-prompts/*.md` must be reworded to match the new defaults. That's a code-step job.

- `.claude/reference/scope/container-environment/index.md`: `#description`, `#runtime`, `#missing-podman`, `#podman-machine`, `#image`, `#mounts` (`#spec`, `#question`, `#code`), `#paths`, `#volumes`, `#logging-in`, `#guards`, `#spec-build`
